content: Originally released in The Interline’s AI Report 2026 , this executive interview with Bamboo Rose is one of a 17-part series that sees The Interline quiz executives from companies who have either introduced new AI solutions or added meaningful new AI capabilities into their existing platforms . For more exclusive interviews, stories and opinions from different industry perspectives, and real survey feedback from voices from every level of fashion, download The AI Report 2026 . We’re observing a big disconnect (in both our own fashion-only data and in wider benchmarks from other sources) between the increasing capability and reliability of AI, in both a general sense and in discrete applications, and the lack of trust that end users place in its outputs. What does trust in your specific applications of AI look like, and how do you achieve and measure it? Trust in enterprise retail AI isn’t about blind faith; it’s about transparency and context. The trust gap exists because users are frequently handed “black box” recommendations without any visibility into how they were generated. If an AI tells a sourcing manager to switch suppliers or alters a demand forecast by 20%, the natural human reaction is skepticism. To break that down, we treat our AI as a performance co-pilot rather than an opaque decision-maker. We achieve trust through data lineage and identical governance. Our Metadata Layer (MDL) ensures that whether an AI agent or a human is looking at product data, they are bound by the exact same permissions, regulatory parameters, and compliance rules. content: Textile Genesis arranged an exclusive workshop today, bringing together suppliers to discuss their experience with the Textile Genesis platform and gather ideas on how it can be improved for everyday use. The session drew a mixed group of participants, including traders and manufacturers, working with both sustainable and conventional materials — giving the discussion a fairly rounded picture of how different supply chain actors are using the platform. Speaking at the workshop, Textile Genesis Regional Lead Shahana Kiron said supply chain members are a key source of ideas for improvement, and that Textile Genesis is closely working to resolve supplier issues by arranging this kind of event. She added that the workshop itself reflects the importance the company places on supplier engagement. Throughout the session, Customer Success Manager Afroza Akter Shimu walked participants through the platform, sharing practical tips to help suppliers navigate common problems they face while using it. Figure: Shahana Kiron, Regional Lead & Advisor, TextileGenesis™. Suppliers responded to the initiative with enthusiasm, and several requested that Textile Genesis organize more in-person workshops of this kind, so they can continue engaging directly with their supply chain members. The day wrapped up with a group photo session, as participants exchanged thanks with one another before heading out.

content: Manchester Fashion Week returns with a four-day programme held from September 9-12 2026 across the city’s St John’s neighbourhood, uniting designers, brands, manufacturers, educators and innovators around an industry under pressure to change. The programme is organised around a set of problems the sector has been slow to confront. The day will move through regenerative materials and next-generation animal-free innovation, before confronting the realities of fashion’s global workforce and how environmental progress can be made without displacing the livelihoods that depend on it. content: Bangladesh does not grow cotton. Yet water may ultimately decide the country’s competitiveness in global denim sourcing. Before diving deeper, it is important to recognize that freshwater represents only 2.5% of the world’s water, and we are doing everything with this limited resource. Of that 2.5%, only approximately 33% is available for daily uses such as drinking, washing, and textile processing. This apparent contradiction reveals a deeper truth about sustainability in textiles: carbon emissions in denim manufacturing are not generated in isolation, they are driven by water. Water that is pumped, heated, circulated, treated, and discharged consumes enormous amounts of energy. In Bangladesh, where denim production is heavily dependent on wet processing and fossil fuel-based utilities, water has become the hidden engine of carbon emissions. content: Key insights August merchandise exports rose 13.14% year-on-year to $4.43 billion. RMG exports increased 13.92% to $3.61 billion, led by knitwear. August exports fell 6.30% from July despite the annual rebound. RMG contributed 81.47% of total export earnings in August. A low August 2025 base amplified this year’s headline export growth. Figure: RMG exports increased 13.92% to $3.61 billion, led by knitwear. Bangladesh’s merchandise exports rebounded strongly in August , but the headline growth masks a more complicated picture for manufacturers. Export earnings rose 13.14% year-on-year to $4.43 billion from around $3.92 billion a year earlier, according to the latest Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data. The recovery came mainly from the readymade garment (RMG) sector, while several non-RMG industries also recorded double-digit growth. However, the monthly picture was weaker. August exports were 6.30% lower than July’s $4.73 billion. This indicates that the annual increase was not driven by a continuous month-on-month acceleration. Instead, a weak base in August 2025 played an important role in lifting the year-on-year growth rate. Table 1. Bangladesh’s RMG export performance in August 2026 Category August 2025 ($ Billion) August 2026 ($ Billion) Growth Rate (YoY) Knitwear 1.77 2.03 +14.88% Woven garments 1.40 1.57 +12.70% Total RMG 3.17 3.61 +13.92% Total exports 3.92 4.43 +13.14% Source: Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) and BGMEA. Together, the two garment segments accounted for 81.47% of Bangladesh’s total merchandise export earnings in August. The result is notable because manufacturers were operating under severe energy constraints. summary: The European Union’s Digital Product Passport (DPP) is creating a new opportunity for African textile and apparel manufacturers to improve traceability, circularity and access to the European market....
content: The European Union’s Digital Product Passport (DPP) is creating a new opportunity for African textile and apparel manufacturers to improve traceability, circularity and access to the European market. Figure:EU’s Digital Product Passport creates new opportunity for African textiles The European Commission launched the DPP Registry and testing environment on July 20, 2026, marking a major step toward making the system operational for businesses. The Registry will record unique product identifiers, registration data and key metadata, while detailed product information will remain with economic operators or their DPP service providers. For textile and apparel companies, the development is important because the sector is one of the EU’s priority product groups under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR). The European Commission currently expects to adopt the textile-specific ESPR delegated act in the fourth quarter of 2027. A DPP could provide information on a garment’s product identification, fiber composition, origin, relevant economic operators, repair and maintenance, reuse, recycling and end-of-life management. A QR code or another data carrier on the product can provide access to the required information. For African manufacturers, this shift could turn sustainability compliance into a competitive opportunity. Better digital records can help exporters demonstrate product origin, material composition and environmental performance while building stronger links with European buyers. The opportunity is particularly relevant as African textile producers seek to expand their role in global value chains. content: BY IWTO BRUSSELS – Two major pieces of EU legislation are moving into implementation at the same time, and textiles sit at their intersection. Member States must transpose the revised Waste Framework Directive, which requires textile Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) schemes to be established by April 2028. Meanwhile, the European Commission is developing textile-specific rules under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR), including requirements for a Digital Product Passport (DPP). The two frameworks are designed to work together. Under the Waste Framework Directive, producer contributions are based on product weight and, where appropriate, quantity – the number of products placed on the market. These contributions finance collection, sorting, reuse, recycling and other end-of-life responsibilities. Fees must then be eco-modulated using relevant sustainability and circularity criteria developed under ESPR or other harmonised EU rules. This is an important step. But there is still a missing piece: evidence of what happens to garments in real life. Ecodesign rules are necessarily set before a product is sold. They therefore use tests, product characteristics and assumptions to predict durability, recyclability and likely lifetime. Yet technically durable clothing is not always worn for a long time. Fit, care, fashion cycles, price, resale and many other factors influence when a garment leaves use. Prediction is necessary, but it should not be mistaken for proof. A practical feedback loop IWTO proposes adding the year of production to the textile Digital Product Passport. Combined with statistically robust waste audits, this would allow authorities to see how quickly – or slowly – different categories of garments enter collection and waste streams.

title: DeSL Launches Digital Product Passport Software Built on PLM
summary: New functionality enables brands to create, govern and publish Digital Product Passports using product, supplier, quality and certification data managed in DeSL PLM The post DeSL Launches Digital Product Passport Software Built on PLM appeared first on The Interline .
content: (New York, NY, September 2, 2026) Discover e-Solutions (DeSL), a provider of Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) solutions for the fashion, apparel, footwear and retail industries, today announced the launch of its Digital Product Passport (DPP) solution. The new functionality enables brands to create and publish Digital Product Passports directly from the product, supplier, quality and certification information managed within DeSL PLM . As Digital Product Passport requirements continue to develop, brands face the challenge of bringing together product information, material and supplier data, certifications, quality records and supporting documentation from across the supply chain. DeSL’s approach uses PLM as the foundation for managing and governing that information throughout the product lifecycle. Rather than creating a separate static record, DeSL generates each passport from the current approved information held within the platform. This allows information presented to consumers, retail partners and other stakeholders to remain connected to its underlying product and supplier records, including version history and approvals. The solution brings together product specifications, materials, supplier information, declarations, inspections and certifications. DeSL’s AI document intelligence can also analyze supporting documents, identify required information and expiration dates, and compare documentation against information maintained within PLM. summary: The 10th Print Tech Bangladesh will bring printing technology suppliers, manufacturers and industry buyers together in Dhaka from September 24–26, 2026. The three-day trade show will take place at the...
content: The 10th Print Tech Bangladesh will bring printing technology suppliers, manufacturers and industry buyers together in Dhaka from September 24–26, 2026. The three-day trade show will take place at the International Convention City Bashundhara (ICCB). The event will showcase technologies and solutions for textile and garment printing, digital printing, screen printing and sublimation printing. It will also cover pre-press, print finishing, postpress, inks, consumables, software, labels and paper converting. The exhibition comes as Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry looks to improve product value, flexibility and production efficiency. New printing technologies can help manufacturers meet demand for customized designs, shorter production runs and faster turnaround. Visitors will include textile and garment manufacturers, exporters, factory owners, purchase managers, production professionals, R&D teams, quality controllers, brand managers, label printers and packaging professionals. Print Tech Bangladesh has previously been held in 2023, 2024 and 2025. The 2026 edition will mark its 10th edition, bringing a wider range of printing and related technologies under one platform. With printing playing a growing role in apparel value addition and product differentiation, the exhibition is expected to offer Bangladesh’s manufacturers a platform to assess technologies that can support the next stage of industry growth.

CAMX 2026 – the Composites and Advanced Materials Expo – will take place from September 21-24, at the Georgia World Congress Centre in Atlanta, Georgia. Developed using Vectis, James Cropper’s proprietary fibre alignment technology, Unimat is a highly aligned discontinuous carbon fibre material engineered from recycled and production-induced waste carbon fibre feedstocks. It was developed through a strategic collaboration between James Cropper Advanced Materials and Carbon Fiber Recycling (CFR) in the UK, creating a scalable pathway for transforming carbon fibre waste into high-value composite reinforcement. The nomination highlights a significant industry achievement, demonstrating that recycled carbon fibre can deliver the performance, consistency and manufacturing readiness required for demanding composite applications, without sacrificing sustainability goals. Working alongside industry partners committed to improving sustainability within aerospace, Carbon Fiber Recycling applies its proprietary recovery and refinement technologies to transform carbon fibre waste into a high-quality feedstock. content: The 65th Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress (Dornbirn GFC) will open on September 16 th in the Austrian town, with a high-level programme bringing together senior representatives from across the European fibres, textiles and nonwovens industries to address the technological, regulatory and economic forces reshaping the sector. Beginning at 9am in Hall A, the opening session will set the scene for the congress with perspectives on innovation, sustainability, circularity, European competitiveness and the continuing transformation of the fibre industry. Managing director of the congress, Béatrice Moureaux will officially open proceedings before Robert van de Kerkhof, president of the Austrian Fibers Institute, addresses the importance of innovation and the methodologies increasingly influencing the direction of the textile industry. A former Lenzing board member with extensive international experience in fibres and sustainability, van de Kerkhof will examine how developments including the European Green Deal and Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) methodology are helping shape future priorities for the industry. Demanding objectives The European fibre sector’s changing competitive environment will provide another major focus of the morning. content: India’s PI Cottex is planning further investment in finishing technology as it looks to increase production capacity from around 600 to 1,000 tons per month over the next two-to-five years. The Ludhiana-based company already operates four stenters, including two supplied by Brückner, one a six-chamber system and the other with ten-chambers, and says its experience with the German machinery manufacturer is encouraging it to consider further installations as part of its expansion plans. “The reliable performance, high process reliability and consistently high quality of the finishing results gave us the confidence to invest in Brückner technology again,” says PI Cottex managing director Jasdeep Singh. He points in particular to the dryer design of the Brückner machines, which enables certain processes to be carried out with fewer chambers while maintaining the required results. Other benefits include high production output, consistent heat-setting, improved shrinkage control and reduced energy consumption. Control parameters The investments form part of the continuing development of PI Cottex from a traditional contract finisher into a vertically integrated knitted fabric manufacturer. The company now carries out knitting, dyeing and finishing in-house, providing control over parameters including colour shade, fabric weight and width, shrinkage and hand feel. Its portfolio includes single jersey, piqué, terry, fleece, rib, interlock and waffle fabrics, along with activewear materials, primarily based on cotton and cotton-elastane blends. It also develops fabrics to individual customer requirements in terms of weight, width, fibre blend, colour and finish. content: Ten innovators developing new technologies, materials and business models for the fashion and textile industries have been selected as finalists for the ninth Avantex Fashion Pitch. The international competition, organised by Messe Frankfurt France, culminates on 31 August 2026 with a Grand Finale in the Agora at Texworld Apparel Sourcing Paris. The finalists will present their solutions before a jury comprising investors, industry professionals and fashion innovation specialists. An evening event at Le Balcon, the rooftop restaurant of Galeries Lafayette, will bring together finalists, jury members, partners and invited guests, culminating in the announcement of the 2026 Avantex Fashion Pitch winner. Messe Frankfurt France launched Avantex Fashion Pitch alongside its Avantex Paris trade show to identify emerging solutions with the potential to transform how fashion is designed, manufactured and consumed, while helping their developers gain industry visibility and accelerate growth. The competition is open to start-ups, innovative SMEs, NGOs, researchers and entrepreneurs developing products, services and technologies for the fashion and textile industries, with a particular emphasis on B2B and B2B2C business models. This year’s finalists span services, textile and raw material innovation, and design technologies. content: On September 24 th 2026 at 10am, the organisers of the ITMA 2027 textile machinery show will hold a live webinar entitled From Connected Factories to Competitive Advantage. As technology connects, more machines, processes, data and people across the factory, the next challenge is turning that connectivity into real business advantage. Industry leaders will explore how automation and digital innovation can improve productivity, quality, agility and operational resilience, and how manufacturers can make smarter technology investment decisions. Participants can register here . The rise of the intelligent garment factory is meanwhile the subject of the latest ITMA Blog. Automation challenge Walk into one of today’s large apparel factories and you’ll witness autonomous vehicles, intelligent transport systems, automated warehouses, machine vision and AI-driven production planning. Yet at the centre of all this technology remains a surprisingly familiar sight – banks of operators guiding fabrics through sewing machines. Joining two pieces of textile together continues to be one of manufacturing’s hardest automation challenges. content: A seminar titled “Beyond the Degree: Building a Successful Career in Textile & RMG” was held at Narsingdi Textile Engineering College (NTEC), focusing on career readiness, industry expectations and the skills required to build successful careers in the textile and apparel sector. The seminar featured Sk. Mamun Ferdoush, General Manager (Marketing & Merchandising), Masco Group, who shared industry insights and practical guidance on preparing for professional careers in the textile and RMG industry. The session focused on career readiness and essential skills in the textile and apparel industry, highlighting the growing importance of analytical thinking, effective communication, technology literacy, leadership, creativity and adaptability. According to the speaker, the evolving nature of the textile and apparel industry requires professionals to go beyond academic qualifications and continuously develop the ability to analyse information, communicate effectively, work across functions and adapt to technological and business changes. Strategic career planning The seminar also addressed the importance of developing a strategic career roadmap. Students were encouraged to approach career development as a continuous process involving self-assessment, lifelong learning, personal branding, practical experience and professional networking. The discussion emphasised the need for students to identify their strengths and career interests while developing the technical, interpersonal and professional competencies relevant to their desired career paths. Internships as a bridge to industry Internship preparation and industry exposure were also highlighted during the session. Internships were described as an important bridge between academic knowledge and practical workplace experience.

content: Bangladesh and China are set to launch a new two‑tier diplomacy and defense dialogue. The initiative follows Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s recent visit to China, aiming to further strengthen bilateral ties. The proposed framework was discussed during a meeting between Humaiun Kobir, State Minister, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Chinese Ambassador to Bangladesh Yao Wen at the Foreign Ministry in Dhaka. Figure: Humaiun Kobir, State Minister, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Chinese Ambassador to Bangladesh Yao Wen. The two sides also agreed to work towards launching a foreign minister-level strategic dialogue, seeking to give greater institutional depth to Bangladesh’s relationship with China, its largest trading partner and a major development and infrastructure partner. Kabir described China as a “trusted friend and valued strategic partner” and reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to the one-China principle. He also welcomed renewed momentum in bilateral relations and the elevation of ties to a “China-Bangladesh Community with a Shared Future”. During the meeting, Yao briefed Kabir on the outcomes of Rahman’s China visit, including the innovative of the China Economic and Industrial Zone (CEIZ), the signing of a commercial contract to modernize Mongla seaport and potential Chinese cooperation in establishing a Mongla export-processing zone. The CEIZ is expected to attract around 30 Chinese companies and approximately $500 million in investment, with the potential to create about 100,000 jobs for Bangladeshis. The proposed diplomacy and defense dialogue could broaden bilateral cooperation beyond trade, infrastructure and development to strategic and security-related areas. content: WASHINGTON, D.C. — September 1, 2026 — The American Apparel & Footwear Association (AAFA) celebrates the passage of a two-year extension of the Haiti Economic Lift Program and the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) by the House with bipartisan support. The vote (370-48), which occurred as part of the Continuing Resolution (CR) to temporarily fund the government, provides for a crucial extension of both programs, which were set to expire at the end of this year. Once the CR is signed into law, the programs will expire December 31, 2028. For 25 years, AGOA has provided eligible Sub-Saharan African countries with duty-free access, strengthening American exports in textiles and agriculture and fostering a wide array of U.S.–Africa commercial partnerships. Likewise, for more than 15 years, the Haiti HOPE/HELP programs have supported both U.S. and Haitian textile industries by granting Haiti duty-free access for apparel and textile products, building strong business ties between the two neighboring nations. “We are grateful for the bipartisan, bicameral support these vital programs have received and look forward to President Trump signing the two-year extension into law,” said Beth Hughes, AAFA’s Vice President of Trade and Customs Policy. “Our industry remains firmly committed to these programs and encourages Congress to use this extension as an opportunity to modernize AGOA and Haiti HOPE/HELP and build toward a 15-year renewal. content: Texworld Apparel Sourcing Paris, Europe’s premier trade fair for the textile and apparel industries, opens today at Paris Le Bourget and continues until 02 September 2026, bringing together manufacturers, suppliers, and professional buyers from across the global fashion and textile industry. The 59th edition features around 1,300 manufacturers from approximately 35 countries, offering international buyers a diverse range of fabrics, apparel, accessories, and innovative textile solutions. Figure: Warptex Bangladesh showcases its products to international buyers at Texworld Paris 2026. The exhibition brings together key textile and apparel markets, including Bangladesh, Pakistan, China, India, Türkiye, Myanmar, South Korea, Japan, and Italy. Bangladesh further strengthens its position as the world’s second-largest sourcing hub for finished apparel after China, highlighting its growing importance in the global apparel supply chain. A total of 17 Bangladeshi companies are participating in the fair, with some exhibiting independently and others under the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) Pavilion, representing the country’s strong textile and apparel sector. Among the participating companies are Hoorain High Tech (HTF), NZ Denim, Skylark Knit Composite, Norban Comtex, Warptex, BNM Garments Industry, Fabitex Industries, DK Textile, and several others. Illias, Merchandising Manager at DK Textile, said, “The response at Texworld & Apparel Sourcing Paris 2026 has been very positive so far. content: The Indian terry product manufacturer’s repeat investment highlights the role of finishing performance and local technical support in building long-term machinery partnerships. Kapoor Industries Limited has expanded its installed base of Biancalani AIRO®24 finishing machines to eight units across its manufacturing facilities in India. The repeat investment represents a significant milestone for Italian textile machinery manufacturer Biancalani and strengthens its position in the Indian textile finishing market. Kapoor Industries is one of India’s established manufacturers and exporters of premium terry products, including towels, bath mats, rugs and bathrobes. The company operates vertically integrated manufacturing facilities in Panipat and supplies international customers, primarily in the United States and Europe. As Kapoor Industries has expanded its production capacity, it has continued investing in the AIRO®24 platform to support the finishing requirements of its terry product lines. While an initial machine order can demonstrate interest in a particular technology, repeated investment provides a stronger indication of its performance under industrial production conditions. The presence of eight AIRO®24 machines suggests that the technology has delivered consistent results across multiple stages of Kapoor Industries’ expansion. The system uses controlled high-speed airflow to move fabric alternately through a treatment channel and against specially designed stainless-steel grids. summary: Premium Bulgarian men’s sock brand Zeneri has begun commercial production of a new collection based on its patented three-zone knitted architecture, developed to prevent socks from sliding down the leg while maintaining comfort. content: Premium Bulgarian men’s sock brand Zeneri has begun commercial production of a new collection based on its patented three-zone knitted architecture, developed to prevent socks from sliding down the leg while maintaining comfort. The technology, protected by European Patent EP3998888, is the result of five years of research, development and testing. Zeneri says successive knitting structures and prototypes were evaluated before the company arrived at the three-zone construction now being introduced commercially. The patented architecture takes a different approach to conventional sock retention. Traditional hosiery typically concentrates elastic tension in the welt, creating a relatively narrow high-pressure band at the top of the sock. Zeneri instead distributes support across three knitted zones, with compression decreasing up the leg and a dedicated stability zone positioned at the ankle. According to the company, the ankle zone plays a key role in determining the position of the sock, allowing retention to be achieved through the knitted structure rather than through silicone bands or additional grip finishes. © Zeneri Materials coming into direct contact with the leg are laboratory tested before entering production. Elastic fibres are knitted so they remain wrapped inside the cotton yarn rather than running bare against the skin. Zeneri says this construction enables the graduated compression structure to retain its shape while remaining breathable and avoiding excessive tightness. The socks also feature hand-linked toes. The retention technology has enabled Zeneri to reconsider the traditional length of formal men’s socks. content: HONG KONG — September 1, 2026 — Sustainable and high-performance textile and textile technology developer Schotex Global® Co. Ltd. announces it has named outdoor industry sales veteran Mats Jengard as its head of sales for the Nordic region. Mats Jengard Jengard brings more than 25 years of successful sales and project management experience to his position at Schotex. Based in Sweden, Jengard has served as sales manager for established outdoor performance brands, including Norrona, PrimaLoft and W.L. Gore & Associates. Designed in Switzerland, developed from European raw materials, and manufactured on European machinery, the Schotex Global collection pairs Swiss design heritage with the efficiency of Asian manufacturing. Schotex Global textiles range from its ACTIVE double weave constructions and FLEX single-layer textiles with exceptional 4-way stretch comfort to its TERRA natural fiber and technical synthetic blends and its SHIELD ultimate weather protection 2- or 3-layer laminates. “We see great potential for Schotex in Northern Europe with the addition of Mats to our team, and are excited for him to introduce our product offerings to the outdoor performance brands in his Nordic region,” said Schotex Co-Founder and CEO Gwen Hsu. “His deep experience with global brands, collaborative work style, and focus on guiding long-term partnership programs with exceptional customer service align perfectly with our company goals and working principles. He is also a passionate outdoorsman who understands exactly what our consumers need and look for in their garments.” Outside of work, Jengard enjoys alpine skiing, downhill biking, hiking, as well as golf. content: LOS ANGELES — September 1, 2026 — Tiger Commercial & Industrial (C&I) has completed the sale of a portfolio of high-precision fabrication and assembly machinery and equipment (M&E), along with finished products and raw materials, from two U.S. plants. Conducted on behalf of the secured creditors, the online auction featured M&E from the former Alpharetta, Georgia, and Dallas, Texas, facilities of Auzmet, a national manufacturer of exterior building solutions such as composite metal panels, architectural façades and insulated wall panels. Schlebach Quadro+ standing seam rollforming system Tiger marketed a broad mix of equipment from the two facilities, including CNC routers, electro-mechanical plate shears, CNC folding machines, electro-pneumatic saws, and smart routers by brands such as Miller, Lincoln Electric, FomIndustrie, Schechtl and Schlebach. Bidders in the 415-lot sale vied for plant-support M&E and rolling stock by brands such as Kaesar, Chevy and Mitsubishi, along with raw materials and finished-goods inventory originally valued at more than $1 million. Tiger’s in-house auction and operations team leveraged its proprietary database of repeat buyers in composites manufacturing to drive demand across the offering, managing the entire sale and removal process across both facilities within a tight 30-day deadline set by the landlord. “Our years of experience with aluminum fabrication equipment—including large-format panel builders from AXYZ Automation Group and units from Schechtl and Durma—gave us the ability to execute and quickly monetize the collateral,” said Jonathan Holiday, Senior Director of Tiger Commercial & Industrial. “The end result was a robust recovery for the secured creditors in a fraction of the usual timeframe.” Posted: September 1, 2026 Source:

content: TEMPE, Ariz. — September 1, 2026 — Economic activity in the manufacturing sector expanded in August for the eighth consecutive month, say the nation’s supply executives in the latest ISM ® Manufacturing PMI ® Report. The report was issued today by Susan Spence, MBA, Chair of the Institute for Supply Management ® (ISM ® ) Manufacturing Business Survey Committee. “The Manufacturing PMI ® registered 54.6 percent in August, 1 percentage point below the July figure of 55.6 percent. The overall economy continued in expansion for the 22nd month in a row. (A Manufacturing PMI ® above 47.5 percent, over a period of time, generally indicates an expansion of the overall economy.) The New Orders Index expanded for the eighth consecutive month after four straight readings in contraction, registering 53.7 percent, down 3 percentage points compared to July’s figure of 56.7 percent. The August reading of the Production Index (58.3 percent) is 0.2 percentage point lower than the 58.5 percent recorded in July. The Prices Index remained in expansion (or ‘increasing’ territory), registering 71.1 percent, the same reading as July. The technology being adopted is primarily Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled digital production monitoring and Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) . Sensors connected to sewing machines capture machine status, output, cycle time, and downtime. The system can link operator identification, while centralized dashboards provide real-time visibility into production and quality. content: Germany’s textile recycling sector is facing growing pressure as rising textile waste, contamination and weaker reuse markets challenge the country’s circular economy. Recyclers are struggling with higher operating costs while demand for used textiles and recycled materials remains under pressure. Figure:The German Federation for Secondary Raw Materials and Waste Management (BVSE) is demanding a binding 30% recycled-content quota and reforms to extended producer responsibility (EPR). Germany consumes nearly 19 kg of textiles per person each year, equivalent to about 1.56 million tons of textiles annually. Around 1 million tons of textile waste are collected each year, highlighting the scale of the material flow that needs to be sorted, reused or recycled. The latest industry data shows that the quality of collected textiles has also deteriorated. Contaminants and non-textile waste in collection containers have increased from 10.8% in 2018 to between 15% and 20% today. Higher contamination makes sorting more expensive and reduces the share of material suitable for reuse or recycling. At the same time, the share of collected textiles designated for reuse fell from 62% in 2018 to 44% in 2023. Mechanical and material recycling increased to 35%, while thermal recovery, including incineration, nearly doubled from 12% to 21%. The industry is therefore calling for stronger economic incentives and policy support. The German Federation for Secondary Raw Materials and Waste Management (BVSE) is demanding a binding 30% recycled-content quota and reforms to extended producer responsibility (EPR). content: NEW YORK — September 1, 2026 — Randa Apparel & Accessories (Randa), a global leader in apparel and lifestyle accessories, today announced that it has acquired the UNTUCKit brand and operations. UNTUCKit is a digitally native, New York-based menswear brand with more than 70 retail stores and a substantial e-commerce business. The transaction brings together UNTUCKit’s strong direct relationship with consumers and Randa’s financial strength and global reach to support the brand’s next phase of growth. UNTUCKit Storefront in New Orleans “We spent 15 years proving that a shirt built to be worn untucked could become a brand people trust,” said Chris Riccobono, UNTUCKit’s founder. “Randa brings something different: more than a century of relationships with the world’s leading retailers and suppliers, along with the global capabilities to help UNTUCKit reach its next stage.” Founded in 2010, UNTUCKit built its name on the shirt designed to be worn untucked and grew into a leader in men’s dress and casual shirts, with a direct-to-consumer footprint spanning e-commerce and brick-and-mortar retail. The transaction advances Randa’s strategy of building and investing in leading brands while moving closer to the consumer. “UNTUCKit did the hard thing: it built a direct relationship with the consumer, store by store and click by click,” said Justin Spiegel, President of Randa. “Randa will add capital, global sourcing and market-leading retail relationships to that foundation. Together, we will accelerate the brand’s growth and introduce it to many more consumers.” The UNTUCKit business and its leadership team will continue to operate from its SoHo headquarters in New York City. content: Brazil ended the 2025/26 commercial year with record cotton exports, consolidating its position as the world’s largest exporter and reinforcing its role as a strategic supplier to the global textile industry. Between August 2025 and July 2026, the country exported 3,373,941 tonnes of cotton, an increase of 19% compared with the previous cycle. Export revenues reached a record US$5.3 billion, around 9% higher than in 2024/25, according to ComexStat data compiled by the Brazilian Association of Cotton Growers (Abrapa). The increase represents approximately 538,500 additional tonnes of Brazilian cotton sold overseas during the year. © Abrapa According to Danyella Bonfim, Market Intelligence and Analysis Coordinator at Abrapa, the performance reflects a transformation built over several years, supported by increased production and improvements in the quality, traceability and sustainability of Brazilian cotton. “Brazil has expanded its production and gained scale, while also making progress in quality, traceability and sustainability. This combination has strengthened the competitiveness of Brazilian cotton and, above all, international buyers’ confidence in the country’s ability to supply the market on a regular and consistent basis,” she said. Data from the United States Department of Agriculture, presented in Abrapa’s August report, showed Brazil maintaining its position at the top of the global cotton export rankings. content: Paris, 01/09/2026 – The introduction of the €3 customs duty on low-value imports marks an important milestone in Europe’s efforts to address the challenges created by the rapid growth of ultra-fast-fashion imports. Together with the abolition of the €150 customs duty exemption, it demonstrates that policymakers are willing to act when market distortions become impossible to ignore. But this should be seen as a first step, not the final destination. Today, at Premiere Vision, the European textile and apparel industry reinforced the belief the European Union must now introduce a meaningful handling fee that reflects the real costs generated by billions of direct-to-consumer parcels entering the Single Market every year. A fee in the region of €10 per parcel provides a more realistic indication of the scale required to support effective enforcement. Every parcel entering the EU generates costs. Customs authorities must process declarations, conduct risk assessments and verify compliance. Market surveillance authorities need resources to identify unsafe and non-compliant goods. Product safety checks, logistics handling and enforcement activities all carry a price. Today, a significant portion of these costs is borne by taxpayers and by European companies that already comply with the rules. This is why the debate should not focus solely on trade or taxation. The issue is enforcement. A handling fee should be designed to ensure that those generating these costs contribute to covering them. The initiative is led by the Brazilian Association of Cotton Growers (Abrapa) and the National Association of Cotton Exporters (Anea), with support from the Brazilian Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (ApexBrasil). Held since 2015, the initiative adopted an expanded format this year, bringing together a broader range of stakeholders from across the textile supply chain. In addition to spinners, the program welcomed representatives from brands, retailers, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), research institutes and other strategic stakeholders. Of the 50 participants, 32 represented spinning mills, while 18 represented brands, retailers and NGOs. Two immersion rounds were held in July and August. This broader participation reflects an evolution in the initiative’s approach. Beyond presenting Brazilian cotton to traditional buyers, the Cotton Brazil Dialogues creates a space for direct exchange between those who produce the fiber and those who source, transform, research, influence and make decisions across the supply chain. title: Nanollose targets commercial scale-up of Nullarbor lyocell
title_ko: Nanollose는 Nullarbor lyocell의 상업적 규모 확장을 목표로 합니다.
summary: Australian biomaterials company Nanollose plans to build and operate a pilot-scale microbial cellulose pulp facility in Western Australia to accelerate the commercialization of its Nullarbor lyocell f...
content: Australian biomaterials company Nanollose plans to build and operate a pilot-scale microbial cellulose pulp facility in Western Australia to accelerate the commercialization of its Nullarbor lyocell fiber. The company said the facility will help validate its microbial-cellulose production process at an industry-relevant scale. This replaces an earlier plan to develop pilot and demonstration facilities with external partners. Andrew Moullin, Managing Director, Nanollose, said the company is focusing its near-term strategy on scaling Nullarbor lyocell and proving the technology before moving toward larger commercial arrangements. After validating the process, Nanollose plans to explore licensing, joint ventures or potential sale arrangements. The company does not currently plan to invest directly in full-scale fiber manufacturing. Nullarbor produces microbial cellulose rather than conventional wood-based pulp. The technology aims to provide an alternative feedstock for regenerated cellulosic fibers such as lyocell.

summary: The global fashion industry’s greenhouse gas emissions rose 6.3% in 2024, after a 7.5% increase in 2023. The rise was driven largely by higher fiber production, especially polyester, according to the...
content: The global fashion industry’s greenhouse gas emissions rose 6.3% in 2024, after a 7.5% increase in 2023. The rise was driven largely by higher fiber production, especially polyester, according to the Apparel Impact Institute (AII). Courtesy: Collected Fashion-sector emissions reached roughly 1 gigatons in 2024, equivalent to the total climate footprint of Japan, highlighting growing concerns over the industry’s decarbonization efforts. Kurt Kipka, Chief Impact Officer at AII, described the trend as concerning and linked the increase to greater material consumption across the industry. He also identified cost and availability as major barriers to decarbonization, noting that virgin polyester remains cheaper and more widely available than recycled alternatives. Rising energy prices are adding further pressure. Kipka said volatility caused by the Iran war underscores the need for apparel manufacturers to reduce dependence on oil and gas by adopting renewable energy and onsite battery storage. The industry could also face significant financial consequences if emissions are not reduced. Separate AII research projects a 34% decline in fashion-sector profits by 2030 due to supply-chain disruptions and rising operating costs unless companies take faster action to cut carbon emissions. Despite the challenges, the report highlighted progress in corporate climate commitments. The number of apparel companies with approved science-based climate targets or commitments to establish them increased from around 100 at the end of 2021 to more than 700 as of June 2026. Several major fashion brands have also reported double-digit emissions reductions and increased their use of recycled fibers in garments. title_ko: Filo66의 Made In Filo: 공급망을 기념하는 패브릭 컬렉션
summary: BIELLA, Italy — September 1, 2026 — The eagerly awaited “Made in Filo” collection is once again on show at the 66th edition of Filo. The fabric collection is designed and created by Filo with the aim of showcasing the potential developments of the materials exhibited at the fair to Filo visitors. “Made in Filo,” […]
content: BIELLA, Italy — September 1, 2026 — The eagerly awaited “Made in Filo” collection is once again on show at the 66th edition of Filo. The fabric collection is designed and created by Filo with the aim of showcasing the potential developments of the materials exhibited at the fair to Filo visitors. “Made in Filo,” now in its fourth edition, is a unique initiative among international trade fairs. To implement it, Filo has taken on the challenging task of “going into production itself.” The result is a collection of fabrics created from materials provided by exhibitors, which emphasizes the technical aspects of both the yarns used and the processes employed. The project, along with Filo, involves exhibitors and several partner companies. This edition focuses on the three souls of “Botanica”, the theme of Filo66’s product development proposals, available on Filo website, filo.it. For “Spontaneous,” very simple yarns were used, but they lend a more natural feel to the fabric. “Expanded” embodies the concept of an Italian garden, with very subtle weaves and effects. “Hybridised” gives free rein to the imagination, with highly structured jacquards and much more technical yarns. The “Made in Filo” fabric collection will be exhibited at the 66th edition of Filo in an area specifically dedicated to research and innovation. A preview can be seen in this short presentation video here: https://filo.it/made-in-filo-la-collezione-di-tessuti-che-esalta-la-filiera/ The 66th edition of Filo will take place on September 15 and 16, 2026, at Fiera Milano Rho, Hall 24. content: China’s SAIC‑GM‑Wuling (SGMW) has introduced bamboo‑fibre‑reinforced composites into interior trim components across more than 20 of its production vehicle models, covering eleven part categories including headliners, seat back panels, trunk trim, sun visors and central floor carpets. In collaboration with the International Centre for Bamboo and Rattan (ICBR) and other partners, the development programme addressed three core technical areas – lightweight bamboo fibre manufacturing, fibre‑resin interface bonding and air‑flow/mechanical uniform fibre mat forming. SGMW has established a full industrial chain integrating bamboo growers, fibre processing bases, parts suppliers and vehicle assembly, and has achieved volume production of high‑performance bamboo fibre composite materials. The bamboo fibre composite is manufactured from locally sourced bamboo in Guangxi. An interfacial toughening approach using low‑melting‑point polymers improves fibre‑matrix adhesion, with stepped pressure profiles during moulding reducing void content. An air‑flow and mechanical spreading technique enables uniform mat forming for continuous production. The finished panels contain 75% or more bamboo fibre by weight, with a density around 0.5 g/cm³ which is significantly lower than conventional engineering plastics, and a flexural modulus of 257.3 MPa, meeting automotive interior requirements. A deep‑draw compression process enables forming depths exceeding 25cm, addressing the limited flowability of natural fibres in complex three‑dimensional geometries. The material exhibits near‑zero formaldehyde emissions, reduces carbon emissions by approximately 0.55 kg per kilogram of material compared with conventional plastics, and degrades more than 90% within 360 days under natural conditions. content: NEWARK, CA. — September 1, 2026 — CreateMe Technologies, an AI robotics company pioneering automated apparel manufacturing through advanced bonding and robotics, today announced three key leadership appointments as it enters its next phase of commercialization. John W. Jacobson joins as vice president of commercialization, Leslie Lambert as vice president of people & business operations, and Ashley Nicole Stickler has been promoted to vice president of marketing & partnerships. The appointments strengthen CreateMe’s commercial, operational and brand-building expertise at a pivotal time, as the company advances from technology development and early brand partnerships into broader commercial deployment of its automated manufacturing platform. John W. Jacobson John W. Jacobson joins in the newly created role of vice president of commercialization, bringing nearly two decades of experience building businesses across retail and global manufacturing. He previously co-founded Luminara Worldwide, scaling the business to more than $100 million in retail revenue and 30,000 retail outlets worldwide within six years. In his new role, Jacobson will lead commercialization strategy and work with brands, retailers and manufacturing partners to move programs from development through scaled production. Leslie Lambert Leslie Lambert joins as vice president of people & business operations, bringing more than 20 years of experience building and leading people functions across manufacturing, retail and consumer brands, including Ampersand Brands, CIRCA of America, Sephora and Williams-Sonoma. At CreateMe, she will lead people and business operations and build the talent, organizational, and workforce infrastructure needed to scale CreateMe’s apparel manufacturing platform.
